items.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S9333

SPONSOR: RAMOS
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the executive law, the alcoholic beverage control law,
the banking law, the cannabis law, the civil practice law and rules, the
civil rights law, the civil service law, the correction law, the domes-
tic relations law, the economic development law, the education law, the
environmental conservation law, the general business law, the general
city law, the judiciary law, the labor law, the mental hygiene law, the
parks, recreation and historic preservation law, the penal law, the
public authorities law, the public health law, the real property law,
the retirement and social security law, the surrogate's court procedure
act, the social services law, the tax law, the transportation law, the
volunteer ambulance workers' benefit law, the volunteer firefighters'
benefit law, the workers' compensation law, the facilities development
corporation act, the medical care facilities finance agency act, and the
New York state urban development corporation act, in relation to replac-
ing instances of the terms "alien" and "illegal alien" with the terms
"noncitizen" and "undocumented noncitizen"

 
PURPOSE OF THE BILL:

To coincide with New York's inclusive and welcoming platform on immi-
gration matters, the terms "alien" and "illegal alien" should be removed
from all statutes. By replacing these terms with "noncitizen" and
"undocumented noncitizen," New York will both match the language antic-
ipated to be in federal codes and demonstrate respect and humanity to
its immigrant population.

 
SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Section 1 of the bill provides for the legislative intent behind the
proposal, which supports the purpose statement noted in this memo.

Sections 2 through 98 of the bill propose changing the terms from
"alien" or "illegal alien" to "noncitizen" and "undocumented noncitizen"
in the following consolidated laws: sections 8, 310, 314, 821, and 940
of the Executive Law; section 126 of the Alcoholic Beverage Control Law;
sections 100-A and 633 of the Banking Law; section 87 of the Cannabis
Law; sections 209 and 212 of the Civil Practice Law and Rules; section
12 of the Civil Rights Law; sections 45, 53, and 85 of the Civil Service
Law; section 147 of the Correction Law; section 115-a of the Domestic
Relations Law; section 210 of the Economic Development Law; sections
305, 355, 661, 692, 3001, 6206, 6301, 6305, 6455, 6506, 6524, 6554,
6604, 6604-b, 6609, 6704, 6711, 6805, 6955, 7206, 7206-A, 7324, 7504,
and 7804 of the Education Law; section 52-0113 of the Environmental
Conservation Law; sections 41 and 184-A of the General Business Law;
section 10 of the General City Lar; sections 253 and 460 of the Judici-
ary Law; sections 21 and 590 of the Labor Law; section 67.01 of the
Mental Hygiene Law; section 3.23 of the Parks, Recreation and Historic
Preservation Law; section 400 of the Penal Law; sections 1020-v, 1045-x,
1048x, 1115-x, 1197-q, 1199-v, 1266-c, 1974-d, 2050-v, 27999-gggg, and
2879 of the Public Authorities Law; sections 268-a and 3421 of the
Public Health L aw; sections 10, 15, 16, 321, and 336 of the Real Prop-
erty Law; section 176 of the Retirement and Social Security Law;
sections 307, 401, 707, 1119, 1120, 1415, and 2218 of the Surrogate's
Court Procedure Act, sections 117, 122, 131-k, 158, 209, 369-gg, and
398-e of the Social Services Law; sections 651, 658, and 1304-C of the
Tax Law; section 428 of the Transportation Law; section 17 of the Volun-
teer Ambulance Workers' Benefit Law; section 17 of the Volunteer Fire-
fighters' Benefit Law; and sections 17, 24-a, 25-b, 50, and 121-a of the
Workers Compensation Law.

Sections 99 through 101 of the bill propose changing the terms from
"alien" or "illegal alien" to "noncitizen" and "undocumented noncitizen"
in the following unconsolidated laws: the Facilities Development Corpo-
ration act; the Medical Care Facilities Finance Agency Act, and the New
York State Urban Development Corporation Act.

Section 102 provides for an immediate effective date.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

Currently, under the United States Immigration and Nationality Act and
United States Code, the commonly used term "alien" refers to any person
who is not a citizen or national of the United States. Although hundreds
of years of migration has contributed to the social, economic, and poli-
tical foundations of the United States, a divide between "us" and "them"
has remained crucial to the restriction of people's migration into the
U.S. and immigrant inclusion within the U.S. This divide is expressed,
among other ways, through language. The literal words used by our
government through laws and regulations influence social discourse and
immigration policies. Scholars and politicians alike have criticized the
connotations associated with the term "alien" in federal and state laws
and regulations, as synonymizing foreign-born people with criminals and
outsiders. Not only do these connotations dehumanize the immigrants that
elevate our cultural, civic, and economic life, but they hold power in
the creation of xenophobic laws and rules resulting from legislation and
judicial decisions.

The term "alien" has held roots in U.S. immigration policy since the
first Naturalization Act of 1790. The term has since been ingrained
beyond federal immigration policy into general federal and state laws,
policies, and regulations. While this term is pervasive throughout the
United States, there has been repeated efforts including a recent push,
across the nation, to replace the term with more updated and inclusive
language.

In 2016, the American Library Association and the Library of Congress
revised all subject headings containing the term "alien" and "illegal
alien" to state "non-citizen" and "unauthorized immigration," respec-
tively. The terms' close association with racist sentiments and deroga-
tory connotations motivated the official change. Many other states and
organizations have similarly called for the words to be removed from
official documentation due to the terms' dehumanizing overtones.
Further, national campaigns such as "drop the 1-word" and " WordsMatter"
have launched a call for an end to using the terms "illegal" and
"alien." These movements labeled the term as "lacking precision" and
insensitive.

Various states and state legislators have demonstrated a will to rid
their laws of the term. In January 2016, California removed the term
"alien" from state labor codes. In September 2021, Assembly Bill (AB)
1096 was signed into law, which replaced the outdated and derogatory
term "alien" used to describe noncitizens in California State code.  In
April 2021, Colorado enacted House Bill 21-1075, which replaces "illegal
alien" in state public contracts with "worker without authorization."

Following the recent change in administration, the federal government
has shown intent to produce a more inclusive environment for immigrants
throughout the United States. President Joe Biden introduced the U.S.
Citizenship Act of 2021 on January 20, 2021 as the first step in a
series of immigration reform attempts. Amongst other things, the Act
offers new pathways to citizenship, a review of border controls, support
for asylum seekers, and calls for the replacement of the term "alien"
with "noncitizen" in federal immigration laws. The bill was introduced
to the senate by Senator Bob Mendez and to the House by Congresswoman
Linda Sanchez on February 18, 2021. The White House refers to the bill
as restoring "humanity and American Values to our immigration system."
Further, the directors of ICE and CBP have issued memoranda updating
terminology to be used for communications and materials. Both memos
issued guidance to replace numerous terms used to describe immigrants:
the memos call for term "alien" to be replaced with "noncitizen" or
"migrant." They also replace the terms "illegal alien" and "assim-
ilation" with "undocumented noncitizen" and "civic integration," respec-
tively.

 
PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

None.

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

None.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
Immediate.

summary: Replaces the terms "alien" and "illegal alien" with the terms "noncitizen" and "undocumented noncitizen".
